Hunger is in fact an aid to memorisation: the poor are more retentive than others and the rich are the least retentive of people. Memorisation is an important and indispensable means of knowledge, and for this reason God, glorified and exalted, undertook to His Messenger, may God bless him and grant him peace, to preserve the Qur'an for him: {Do not move your tongue with it to hasten it; indeed upon Us is its gathering and its recitation. So when We have recited it, follow its recitation. Then indeed upon Us is its clarification} (Sūrat al-Qiyāmah 75:16–19). Likewise the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, urged memorisation from him, and ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab likewise urged memorisation in what people transmit.

Al-Shafiʿi, may God have mercy on him, said: proper conduct is that you write down the best of what you have heard, and memorise the best of what you have written, and relate the best of what you have memorised. So he made it three ranks: first, that you write the best of what you have heard; second, that you memorise the best of what you have written; third, that you relate the best of what you have memorised — each rank selected from the one above it. And he said, may God have mercy on him:

*My knowledge is with me wherever I turn; it follows me. My heart is its vessel, not the hollow of a chest.*

*If I am in the house, knowledge is in it with me; or if I am in the market, knowledge is in the market.*

And Abu Muhammad ʿAli ibn Hazm al-Zahiri, may God Most High have mercy on him, says:

*Though they burn the paper, they will not burn what the paper contained; it is rather in my breast.*

*It travels with me wherever my mounts set out, and it stays if I stay, and it will be buried in my grave.*

The scholars used to say: what the book-case holds is not knowledge; knowledge is only what the breast holds. So the broad shelves with many coloured books on them are not knowledge; knowledge is only what the breast holds. Therefore a person needs the instruments of memorisation and the strengthening of that in his mind, so that this may increase him in insight and skill and in gathering the scattered parts and edges of knowledge; and that is accomplished only by hunger at the stage of memorisation.

What is meant by that is moderation in the matter. It is not meant as tormenting the self and starving it, nor as reducing food to the point that it becomes harmful to a person and a diminishing of his strength or a means to his illness. Rather what is meant is that a person be moderate in that and not make this his greatest concern, and that he not spend the best of his time in obtaining his food; rather the best of the time must be what he spends in obtaining knowledge.

THE FIFTH condition is realising the importance of knowledge, which is that a person should hold himself cheap for the sake of gathering knowledge. For whoever does not realise the importance of a thing cannot occupy himself with it, since whoever is ignorant of a thing is hostile to it. That is why you find that many people, when they have tasted the taste of knowledge, become absorbed in it and it delights them, until many others who have not tasted the taste of knowledge consider them men of obsession who have plunged into a matter in which they ought to have kept to the middle and not exceeded. The fact is that they have tasted this taste and the others have not tasted it; or that they have seen this flash and others have not seen it. For this reason Moses, peace be upon him, held himself cheap for the sake of knowledge and rode the sea in a holed ship. One of the scholars said of old:

*The questions of Sahnun said to their reader: you will not attain knowledge until you lick aloes.*

*Knowledge is not attained by an idler, nor by a sluggard, nor by one easily bored, nor by one who keeps company with people.*

"The questions of Sahnun" is al-Mudawwanah, and people used to memorise it as they memorise al-Fātiḥah. "Until you lick aloes" — that is, until you lick what is intensely bitter. But for all that, patience under slight weariness brings a person afterwards to attain stations he would not have attained without this, as the sage said: *No face has become white by the gaining of a noble thing until it was first darkened by the pallor of the quest.*

So if you see one whose face has become white by any noble thing, know that that was preceded by weariness and toil.

THE SIXTH condition is disobeying desire. For one who lets his soul follow its desire must be afflicted with wishful thinking and suspicions; while one who does not follow desire, when his soul inclines to anything, calls it to account for it and holds it under suspicion in it — this is the one who is able to gather knowledge. That is why Abu ʿAsim al-Nabil, when he was hearing hadith from Shuʿbah, and the elephants came to the land of Kufa in the countryside of Iraq and the students of hadith went out to look at the elephants — Shuʿbah said to Abu ʿAsim: Will you not go out to the elephants? He said: I did not come to see the elephants; I came only to write hadith. So he nicknamed him "the Noble" because of that. And al-Suyuti, may God have mercy on him, mentions that he had a window overlooking the Nile, and that when the Nile flooded people would come to it from distant lands to see its flood; and he remained sixteen years without opening the window to see the Nile, because of his occupation with knowledge — sixteen years. So a person must try not to follow desire, even in permissible matters, so that he may attain knowledge in exchange for that.

THE SEVENTH condition is acting upon it. For knowledge, as Ibn ʿUyaynah said, calls out for action: if it answers it, well; otherwise it departs. So whoever does not act upon what he knows, it is a proof against him; and whoever acts upon what he knows, God grants him knowledge of what he did not know. God Most High says: {O you who believe, if you are mindful of God He will make for you a criterion} (Sūrat al-Anfāl 8:29). And the criterion is that by which a person distinguishes between truth and falsehood, and it is a knowledge bestowed directly from God.

Al-Bukhari and Muslim brought out in the two Ṣaḥīḥs, and others, from the hadith of Abu Juhayfah al-Suwaʾi, may God be pleased with him, who said: We said to ʿAli ibn Abi Talib, may God be pleased with him: Do you have anything that you recite other than the Book of God? He said: By Him who split the seed and created the soul, we have nothing that we recite other than the Book of God and what is in this sheet — or an understanding that God grants to a man among His servants. And he brought out the sheet from the scabbard of his sword, and in it was the blood-money, and the ransoming of the captive, and that a Muslim is not killed for an unbeliever, and: Medina is a sanctuary from ʿĀʾir to such-and-such, and whoever commits an offence in it or shelters an offender, upon him is the curse of God and of the angels and of all people; God will not accept from him any obligatory or voluntary act. And whoever claims a father other than his own, or affiliates to other than his own patrons, upon him is the curse of God and of the angels and of all people; God will not accept from him any obligatory or voluntary act … and so on.

The point of citation in the hadith is ʿAli's words "or an understanding that God grants to a man among His servants". This understanding is the knowledge bestowed directly, and it is the second side of knowledge. For knowledge divides into two kinds: knowledge by jidd (earnest effort) and knowledge by jadd (good fortune). The knowledge that is by earnest effort is what is attained by striving and expenditure; and knowledge by good fortune, that is by felicity, is that with which God makes felicitous whomever He wills of His servants, and it is a result of action. The divine lights and the outpourings which the devoted worshippers attain often fill a great gap in the field of knowledge. God Most High has said: {And David and Solomon, when they gave judgement concerning the tillage, when the sheep of the people strayed into it at night; and We were witnesses to their judgement. And We gave Solomon understanding of it; and to each We gave judgement and knowledge} (Sūrat al-Anbiyāʾ 21:78–79). This granting of understanding is a divine outpouring and a divine light which God cast into the heart of Solomon, so that by it he understood God's ruling.

ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab, may God Most High be pleased with him, used to say: O God, I seek refuge with You from a difficult case for which there is no Abu Hasan — meaning ʿAli, may God be pleased with him; for he used to solve the difficult cases. Whoever reads his life, may God be pleased with him, knows that much of the knowledge he had was not among the acquired sciences that human beings reach by striving and seeking; rather it must be a knowledge bestowed directly and divinely, arising from acting upon what he learned and from an increase of faith and God-consciousness and scrupulousness. For he, may God be pleased with him, was one day on the pulpit, and a man stood up and said: a man has died leaving a wife, two parents and two daughters. And ʿAli — and he was in the middle of a sermon rhyming in ʿayn — said: her eighth has become a ninth. The beginning of his sermon was: Praise be to God, who recompenses every soul for what it strives for, and to Him is the return and the coming back. So the questioner asked

about this, and he said: her eighth has become a ninth. From that time it has been known as "the pulpit inheritance case" (al-farīḍah al-minbariyyah), and in it he set out the increase of twenty-four to twenty-seven. For twenty-four is the third of the bases that admit of increase, and its increase is one: it increases only to twenty-seven and nothing else increases. This was not known before this occasion — it was not known in Islam before that occasion — and he produced it with this spontaneity and this speed and said: her eighth has become a ninth.

These seven conditions one of the scholars versified in a single line, saying:

*For it: go abroad, and be humble, and be scrupulous, and be hungry, and be weak, and disobey your desire, and follow.*

Knowledge is of many kinds, and among the greatest of them is the knowledge of practised skill; for knowledge divides into two kinds, the knowledge of receiving and the knowledge of practised skill. The knowledge of receiving means what a person receives from another; and of this kind, some is what he hears and so receives by way of the ear, and some is what he receives by way of writing, and some is what he receives by way of looking and observing alone — all of that is of the knowledge of receiving. As for the knowledge of practised skill, which is the knowledge of training, it is what a person acquires from experience and by which he is able to express what is in his breast and convey his knowledge to another. For how many a person's breast contains much learning but he is unable to express it; and how many a person is a parrot who has come to know learning by rote and repeats it as he took it — "this is our merchandise returned to us". These two kinds are deficient, and the third kind is better, namely the one who develops and adds and improves.

A man saw three doves: one of them swallowed a jewel and brought it out as it was; another swallowed it and brought it out larger than it had been; and another swallowed it and brought it out smaller than it had been. So he asked Muhammad ibn Sirin, may God have mercy on him, about the interpretation of his dream, and he said: you sit in my session, and in the session of Qatadah, and in the session of al-Hasan — these are the leading Successors in Basra at that time. He said: yes. So he said: the dove that swallowed the jewel and brought it out larger than it had been is al-Hasan al-Basri, because he memorises the hadith and then adds to it by his intelligence and his acumen and his understanding and his learning. The one that brought it out as it was is Qatadah, for he memorises the hadith and relates it as it is without addition or omission. And the one that brought it out smaller than it had been is I — meaning himself, Muhammad ibn Sirin — for I have memorised the hadith but I scruple to bring all of it, for fear of adding to it what is not of it.

In general, the one who develops his information and is able to deliver it as is fitting is without doubt better and greater in reward, because there is written for him the rewards of everyone who acts upon what he taught and the rewards of those to whom anything of his learning reached, until the Day of Resurrection, without that diminishing anything of their rewards. This is the aspect in which the predecessors were given precedence over the later generations: that their rewards are not cut off but increase according to the centuries. My teacher, may God have mercy on him, said:

*And every reward attained by the martyrs, or by others such as the scholars and the ascetics,*

*there is attained for the Prophet the like of it, over and above the rewards of what the Prophet himself did,*

*with an additional number that is not bounded and whose count none can reckon but the One;*

*for every guided person and every scholar, until the Day of Recompense, his teacher has attained*

*from the reward the like of the reward of the doer — and likewise from the deficient and the perfect;*

*and his teacher's teacher has twice as much, and fourfold for the third who follows him;*

*and so the doubling of every rank, up to the Messenger of God, of lofty rank.*

*From this is known the precedence of the predecessors and their priority in merit over the later generations.*

Therefore the person who wants to learn must add to that another intention, namely that he should teach what he has learned, because of the words of the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace: "The best of you is he who learns the Qur'an and teaches it." And that is accomplished only by several matters and several means.

The most important of them is the intention of that at the beginning. For one who studies only to learn and understand will make light of many matters and will not take on training and practised skill, because he wants only understanding and passes over that. But one who wants to learn in order to teach will attend to the manners and the conditions and the ways of delivering information and the ways of developing it and of combining it with other information, and to the difficulties that arise with it and the answers to those difficulties; and will apply that to the reality of people, so as to bring solutions for what they are thinking about and for the problems that arise for them; and will look inward into the souls of those present and listening, so as to know which of them has grasped the lesson and which has not. By this he is able to live with the lesson and in its shade. For the intention of teaching, accompanying the intention of learning, is an important matter in this field.

Second, it is necessary after this that a person know that what he will teach must be less than what he has learned: he delivers to his students only a part of what he has, because if he drains everything he has he becomes an empty box. Because of that he will select from what he has the easiest and the smoothest and the most firmly established, and that is what he presents, and he keeps for himself a reserve which he can develop and increase. That is why the people of learning say: knowledge is a sea, and its vessels are like the vessels of water — one scoops with them, and there cannot be a vessel that scoops the whole sea. Therefore a person needs to learn more than he teaches. Whoever wants to explain a particular book must be acquainted with a broader book in the discipline he is in; if you have not read a book broader than this, you will not be able to teach this book.

Hence you hear of many simpletons who venture upon the great encyclopaedias and the mighty books, wanting to explain them, when those are the last thing composed in the discipline — as though they had studied what is broader than them, whereas the reality is otherwise. You find one of them venturing, for example, upon explaining the book of Sibawayh, as though he had studied something broader than it in grammar; or venturing upon teaching al-Muwāfaqāt of al-Shatibi, as though he had studied many of the books of legal theory until he reached this rare quintessence. None will reach this level but the rarest of people, who have combined the rational and the transmitted sciences and have taken on training and gathered many disciplines and sciences. Therefore, God have mercy on one who knows his measure and sits below it. The Arabs say: "Bow your head, Kara; the ostriches are in the villages." So a person should not try to be a raisin before he is a sour grape: let him first try to bring the little before the much.

That is why Ibn ʿAbbas, may God be pleased with them both, said in explaining the words of God Most High "be rabbānīs" (Sūrat Āl ʿImrān 3:79): he said, be scholars, wise men; and in another transmission: the rabbānīs are those who train people with the small matters of learning before the great ones — he tries to bring the small before the great.

For this reason the methods of the people of learning in all the sciences are that they made graded books. Notice that a single author composes several books of differing sizes and differing content, intending by that the differing levels of students. Here is Ibn Qudamah in Hanbali fiqh — and he is the father of this school, its greatest compiler — who composed, for example, al-ʿUmdah for the young, and above it al-Muqniʿ, and above that al-Kāfī, and above that al-Mughnī, each book composed for one level of the students of knowledge. Likewise Ibn Hisham al-Ansari composed in grammar Qaṭr al-Nadā for beginners, and above it Shudhūr al-Dhahab, then above that Iʿrāb al-Jumal wa-mā Yalḥaqu bihā, and above that Awḍaḥ al-Masālik, and above that Mughnī al-Labīb ʿan Kutub al-Aʿārīb — all this by gradation, so that the student of knowledge may proceed by degrees and not take knowledge at random. Many people do not grasp this division and so fall upon the largest books they find, and hold that the small books are of no benefit and are a waste of time, and pass them by.

Likewise, among a person's means for this is to know that the sciences are interlinked and interpenetrating; for knowledge as a whole is like the parts of the body: the blood pumped into the brain is the blood pumped into the leg, the same blood, one circulation. Therefore a person must grasp the secrets of the sciences and their interconnection; and let him know that he cannot be skilled in one of the sciences unless he is acquainted with the sciences that complete it.

The fourth matter is that whoever wants to be a teacher should know that teaching, as we have mentioned, is a practised skill that needs training. So let him begin by teaching alone, imagining that he has before him a person whom he is teaching; he tests himself by that and so knows whether he is capable of explaining or not, whether he has grasped the book or has not grasped it. So he teaches alone, as al-Aʿmash, may God have mercy on him, used to tie up a billy-goat beside him and teach it and say: have you understood? — and al-Aʿmash's billy-goat became famous for that. This has likewise become well known of the Imam al-Dabbas, one of the leading Hanafis: he used to shut himself into his mosque and go over the legal maxims alone. Al-Dabbas, may God have mercy on him, was blind; and a student came who had learned that when he shut the door upon himself he would repeat something, and wanted to hear it. So he hid in a corner of the mosque and heard him going over the legal maxims, and recorded thirty-four maxims of them; and then a cough came upon him and he coughed, and the shaykh fell silent and rose to him and struck him with a stick and put him out of the mosque — but he had already stolen these maxims and went out with them.

Then after this he tries to apply it to his own household, such as his wife and children; for he has applied it upon himself, and at that point he is able to apply it to those nearest to him, with whom there is no formality between him and them — because knowledge needs training and practice. It is in the position of what Ziyad ibn Abihi said: he said, the top of the pulpit is like the back of a horse; it needs discipline. For a horse, when it is first ridden, cannot be ridden except by the strong, and none can discipline and break it but the skilled. So likewise the top of the pulpit: whoever stands upon it and speaks to people must be prepared for that.

For this reason a person at the beginning of his teaching, or the beginning of his preaching, will tremble and shake, and the thread of the information will be cut off from his memory in many cases. Indeed it is related of al-Qabbaʿ, may God have mercy on him, who was one of the orators of Quraysh, that he stood on the pulpit as a preacher, and when he entered upon the sermon he cried out among the people asking for water and said: Give me to drink, give me to drink — from the awe of that position when he saw the eyes looking at him.

A number of orators became famous who were struck dumb at the beginning of the matter. Here is ʿUthman ibn ʿAffan, may God be pleased with him: when he stood upon the pulpit in the first sermon he addressed to people, he remembered that he was standing in the station of the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, and filling his place for the community. So he praised God and extolled Him, and then was unable to produce a single word, and was silent a long time while people looked at him; then he was moved to tears — that is, he wept — and said: You are in greater need of a commander who acts than of a commander who speaks; and if I remain, the sermons will come to you as they should, and God will make after hardship ease. And he asked forgiveness and came down; and it was the most telling of sermons.

Likewise Muʿawiyah, may God be pleased with him, who was forbearing and wise: when he wanted to preach on an important matter he would sit and not stand upon the pulpit, because of the awe of standing; and he is the first who preached sitting — among the things he was first in, may God be pleased with him.

Then a person must know likewise that teaching is forgotten: whoever does not occupy himself with it is like archery. Archery — a person wearies himself in learning it, and if he neglects it for a time his skill in it is diminished. Likewise swimming: a person learns it, and if he neglects it he forgets it. And teaching is likewise. A severe warning has come from the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, about forgetting archery: whoever learns archery and then neglects it and forgets it — a severe warning has come concerning him. So likewise this knowledge is in the position of archery: if you have learned teaching, it has become a practised skill with you, so try not to break off from it in any way.

For this reason many of the people of learning, when they were imprisoned, tried to teach from behind the prison. Here is al-Sarakhsi, who was imprisoned in a well, and the students would gather until his voice reached them, and he dictated to them his book al-Mabsūṭ in its full length from the bottom of a well.

Likewise, at the beginning of his teaching he must know that the student is the pivot of the process, and that he should not burden his mind with what he does not understand and what does not reach him, and should know that the matter will come by degrees; so let him not try to make his own end point the student's starting point. Let him rather recall his own beginning and try to make the student walk along that road. Many people try to bring you the quintessence, the end of what they have reached, and try to make it your own beginning — and this is a thing you cannot reach except with toil and hardship. That is why it is in the transmitted report: "Speak to people with what they understand; do you wish that God and His Messenger be denied?" And: "You never address a people with a speech that their minds cannot reach but that it is a trial for them." So a person must proceed by degrees with his students and not make them leap in leaps, as many people do, for that leads to a split in their personalities and to a pretence of learning in them: they pretend to learning and suppose that they have reached the highest levels while they are still at the beginning of the road; and so he has joined Satan in deluding these people and ruining their lives.

Likewise he must arrange the sciences according to importance; and people's views may differ in the arrangement of the sciences. Among them are those who hold that one should begin with the means before the objectives, because the means are the containers of the objectives: whoever does not know the language and grammar and morphology cannot understand many of the verses of the Qur'an nor grasp the methods of derivation; and whoever does not know legal theory cannot grasp the juristic questions and the ways of deriving them, and so on. And among them are those who hold that what matters is what people are turning to in their own time and what enters into their concerns.

Therefore, among the sciences there is what is important in every age and whose importance does not recede in any age or any place — such as fiqh. This science people always need, however civilisations and circumstances change and however the outcries against it are raised and grow loud; people always need it. And likewise the understanding of the Book of God: a person is supposed to hear it and to read it, and if something in it is difficult for him or he does not understand it, then he needs to ask; and if he asks, he ought to find an answer; and if he does not find it, sin attaches generally, because answering the questioner about the Book of God is a communal obligation (farḍ kifāyah) — there must be in every town someone who answers the questioner about it.

But even so, people cannot be compelled to a particular arrangement of the sciences. We know that they divide into these two kinds: into objectives, which are the original sciences the learning of which is an act of worship of God; and into means, which complete them and are a means to their perfection and a way to their realisation. Many of the people of learning used to try to combine the two sides and so ordered their time for that. But this combining is only for those who devote themselves to knowledge and have no other occupation. For this reason you find that the students of the faculties, who study in a single sitting various subjects and different matters, master neither this nor that and so become a burden on others. Therefore a person, if he is studying, ought to choose a particular science and try to set the time apart for it, and then afterwards to diversify and study another science in sequence, because the sciences are complementary and some of them complete others.

Al-Suyuti said: I never debated one who had a science but that he defeated me, and I never debated one who had several sciences but that I defeated him. For the one who occupies himself with a particular science will have it clear before him and be acquainted with its details more than another; while the one who occupies himself with various sciences at one time has his heart and his effort scattered among these various sciences — unless he devotes himself to this, or unless he makes a lesson in a particular science in the morning, for example, and a lesson in another science in the evening.

Let a person know likewise that of the sciences there are those in which receiving and hearing are indispensable, and those that can be taken by private reading after the necessary preparation for it. As for private reading, its first condition is that a person should have reached a scholarly level at which he is fit for private reading; and not everyone is fit for private reading — this is the first condition. That is why Abu Hayyan, may God have mercy on him, says:

*The inexperienced man supposes that books guide a brother of understanding to the attainment of the sciences;*

*and the ignorant man does not know that in them are places that have bewildered the mind of the discerning.*

*If you aim at the sciences without a teacher, you will stray from the straight path,*

*and matters will become confused for you until you become more astray than Thomas the sage.*

The sciences that need to be received from people and heard are, for example, the science of recitation and the canonical readings, for it must be received from the mouths of men. Likewise hadith: a chain of transmission is indispensable in it. And likewise the complex sciences that need explanation, such as grammar and morphology and prosody and legal theory. As for the sciences that can be received from the bellies of books, such as history and belles-lettres, these can be received from the bellies of books by private reading; for the historical stories generally have their events in sequence and their results set out in their books. And likewise the books of belles-lettres, which are concerned with the expression of ideas and their sequence and with setting out the aspects of noble conduct and what has become famous of silencing replies and beautiful deeds and the expression of that — this runs with the natural disposition, and so a person can read it privately and be content in it with private reading. It is more profitable and better that he also have recourse in it, along with private reading, to mutual rehearsal; and mutual rehearsal is that he should recite to another and hear from him in this field, so that his knowledge may increase and open out in these matters that are taken by private reading.

As for what is received by way of receiving from the shaykhs, a person needs in it selection — that is, recourse to a shaykh who is skilled and has studied several sciences, so as to select for the person what suits him. For it was among the practice of the people of hadith, the matter of selection in transmission;

and likewise selection in the scholarly material a person studies, according to his level. Then after this come the skills particular to each of these sciences, for each of them needs skills peculiar to it for its delivery. Let us begin with them by degrees:

THE QUESTIONS

Question 1: Many people today object to the diversification of the sciences and say that the Companions, may God be pleased with them, and likewise those after them among the Successors and their followers, did not have what we have today of the kinds of sciences such as grammar and morphology and legal theory and rhetoric and the other sciences; and so they call for a return to what the Companions alone were upon and the discarding of everything else. What is your comment?

The answer: knowledge is an invention and is the child of need. Today our circumstances and our whole life differ from the life of the Companions, and you cannot return in your worldly life and your affairs to what the Companions were upon so as to live exactly in the like of what they lived in. If that were possible, then study only what they studied. If you returned to Medina as it was, and your clothes and your mounts and your dwelling and everything you have returned to be like what they had — then yes, study what they used to study. Otherwise, their need did not call for anything like this; for you are in an age in which transactions are in the millions, and the Companions did not know this; and in an age in which communications gather the easts of the earth and its wests, and the Companions did not know this; and in an age in which prices are affected by politics, so that by a mere rumour the price of shares rises or falls, and this was not so in the time of the Companions; and in an age in which people's means of living develop with astonishing speed daily, and the Companions did not know this.

These people are nothing but the likes of those bedouin who, when the science of grammar arose in the Islamic cities, came from their deserts and saw people occupied with these new sciences and found that strange, so that it became a quarrel with them — until one of them says:

*What have I met from these would-be Arabs and from this analogy of their grammar, which they have invented!*

*If I say a fresh rhyme that has a meaning, it contradicts what they have measured and gauged;*

*they say: you have made a solecism; that letter is in the accusative, and that one lowered, and that one raised;*

*and they have set ʿAbd Allah and Zayd at odds and laboured between them, so that the beating and the pain went on.*

*So I said one thing in which is their answer — and speech is where the truth is spoken and followed:*

*not all my speech is to be expounded to you; so take what you understand, and what you do not understand, leave;*

*until I return to a people who were nourished with what I was nourished with, and the mind is one.*

*I was nourished in a land in which the fire of the Magians is not kindled and in which churches are not built,*

*and whose soil no ape or swine treads; but in it are the white antelope and the lion and the hyena.*

The saying of these people also entails that people should go back to fighting with swords instead of tanks and rockets and aircraft, and that they should go back likewise to riding horses and donkeys instead of cars and aircraft; and likewise that they should abandon Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī and Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim — indeed that they should abandon the copies of the Qur'an, because the Companions in the earliest period did not have them. This leads to the demolition of the religion from its foundation and to the ridding of oneself of all its obligations and of everything people have arrived at.

Whoever says this is like one who says that the writing down of hadith is an innovation and that all these books must be burned because they are of the "second scripture", and that everything that has been written down other than the Book of God ought to be burned — so these people would burn the Muwaṭṭaʾ and the two Ṣaḥīḥs and the other books of hadith. There is no doubt that this is manifest misguidance and clear, evident deviation.

Among them is what some of them say: that the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, left the community upon the heart of one man, and then the people of politics came and divided it — and by "the people of politics" he means the Rightly Guided Caliphs, may God be pleased with them; and then afterwards the jurists came and made bad worse — and by them he means the founders of the schools; so he says: instead of the religion being one, it became four religions, Maliki and Shafiʿi and Hanafi and Hanbali. He has understood nothing of the matter at all; he wanted to demolish the religion in his foolishness and his dullness, and so his devices became exposed before everyone. These people too harp on this; and if they returned to themselves they would know that their call entails abandoning the copy of the Qur'an and abandoning the two Ṣaḥīḥs, and going back to girding on swords and riding horses, and conquering the lands with a fresh conquest all over again, so as to go back and emigrate from Medina and then from it conquer Mecca once more and then restore the life of the Companions as it was, complete in all its aspects.

The reality is that all these sciences are from the Book and the Sunnah. The Book came to be a constitution for the Muslims in every time and place and a legislative foundation for them; it was not sent down for the Companions alone, and it cannot be restricted to the understanding of the Companions only. If it were so, the Qur'an would be like other books and its distinction would come to an end. The Qur'an was not sent down for the Companions alone, and its interpretation cannot be restricted to the exegeses of the Companions. If you wanted today to restrict the Qur'an to what has come only from the Companions, and gathered the reports, it would be a small, slight compendium; and you restricted yourself to this and said: this is the meaning of the Qur'an and we do not interpret it beyond this — is this correct? This is the utmost error and charlatanry.

And likewise the other sciences: they are only ramifications of the science of hadith and of the various Qur'anic sciences. These ramifications increase the more people increase in civilisation and the more the sources of their life diversify; and the interpretation of the Qur'an cannot be restricted to what one particular generation understands. For this reason, the people of every age are required to interpret the Qur'an with a new interpretation that suits their reality. And today, if a new exegete comes and is creative, an assault is launched upon him by these backward people, and they say: there is no emigration after the conquest, the exegeses have come to an end, and the exegesis of Ibn Jarir and the exegesis of so-and-so and the exegesis of Ibn Kathir suffice us — as though the Qur'an's meanings had been confined within the understanding of one particular generation or a limited number of generations. The fact is that the people of every age understand from the Qur'an their own share, and there is stored up for them of it what meets their need and sets out their rulings, which arise anew.

The cases that arise anew are without limit; every day there arise cases that never occurred to the Companions — even in the lifetime of the Companions. As soon as the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, died and Abu Bakr took up the affair, many matters arose for the Companions in which they exercised independent reasoning, which had not been in the time of the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace. First, the caliphate did not exist in the time of the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, and had never occurred to them. After that, the grandmother's inheritance is not mentioned in the Book and Abu Bakr did not find it in what he had transmitted of the Sunnah, so he needed to ask people about it.

Then in the caliphate of ʿUmar the like of this arose for him, such as the inheritance of the grandfather along with brothers, when ʿUmar was tried with it in his own family. One of his sons, named ʿAbd al-Rahman, died leaving three sons, and one of them died; and ʿUmar wanted to inherit from him to the exclusion of his two brothers, and it was said to him: you do not inherit from him to the exclusion of his two brothers. He said: how am I a father to him and he is not a son to me? Is it not so that if I died he would inherit from me to the exclusion of my brothers? They said: yes. So he referred the case to the Emigrants and the Helpers, and they made him like one of them. This case became famous, and ʿAli ibn Abi Talib said of it: whoever wants to plunge into the depths of Hell, let him give judgement on the question of the grandfather and the brothers — meaning that it is not governed by a text.

Likewise, in ʿUmar's time there arose the problem of the inheritance of one who kills by mistake: does one who kills by mistake or by quasi-deliberate killing inherit from the one he killed or from his blood-money? It first occurred in the time of ʿUmar, concerning a man of Mudlij who struck his son with a sword and disabled his leg so that he died; and ʿUmar was tried with it and exercised independent reasoning in it.

Likewise the famous ʿUmarid case (al-ʿumariyyah) concerning an estate in which the holders of fixed shares exhausted the property to the exclusion of the full brothers, and among the holders of fixed shares were half-brothers through the mother. So the full brothers came — when it recurred a second time — and said to ʿUmar: do you think that if our father had been a donkey, or a stone cast into the sea, would not the mother still join us? So he made them like the brothers through the mother. Then the first party — those with whom this case had occurred the first time — came disputing, and ʿUmar said to them: that was according to what we judged then, and this is according to what we judge now.

Likewise: does a woman inherit from her husband's blood-money? This question was difficult for ʿUmar, until his crier called out at the hajj: I adjure by God whoever has knowledge from the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, about a woman's inheritance from her husband's blood-money, to come to me. So al-Dahhak ibn Sufyan came to him and said: the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, wrote to me that I should give the wife of Ashyam al-Dibabi an inheritance from her husband's blood-money. And the cases have not ceased to arise anew from that time to this age of ours.

If we went back only to what the Companions had of the sciences, we would neglect all these cases, and that would lead to a shutting-in of the religion and to God's rulings being confined to a limited set of questions beyond which they do not go at all. That is why people blamed the Zahiris in what concerns contracts and transactions; for the Zahiris were rigid in this field and confined usurious gain (ribā) to the six categories mentioned in the hadith of ʿUbadah ibn al-Samit: gold for gold, and silver for silver, and wheat for wheat, and barley for barley, and dates for dates, and salt for salt, like for like, hand to hand, equal for equal; and if these kinds differ, then sell as you wish, so long as it is hand to hand. So they said: there is no ribā except in the six categories. The generality of the Muslims opposed them and brought a broad case against them, because they had confined Islam to a narrow corner, while people's livelihood may be entirely free of these six categories.

Likewise, confining zakat to the properties from which zakat used to be taken in the time of the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, would entail suspending it today. For people's wealth has become these currencies they deal in; so if we said there is no zakat except on grains and fruits and grazing livestock and gold and silver alone, because those are what zakat used to be taken from in the time of the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, that would entail preventing zakat altogether — because most of the rich today own no livestock in which zakat is due, and own neither gold nor silver, and own neither tillage nor cultivation, but own billions of dollars or pounds. So if you were rigid and stopped at this limit, you would prevent zakat and suspend all the interests of Islam. The matter, then, is clear and beyond doubt.

This question enters also into the field of the call to Islam. I met some jurists who objected to this call and said: this that you do and call people to and gather them upon — where did you get it? For we knew our fathers, and they were people of righteousness and scrupulousness and are certainly better than us and than you, and they did not do this that you do. This question they often put to people; and whoever was not wise would begin by reviling their fathers and belittling their judgement and saying that they had not performed the duty — and that became a cause of rancour and hatred without result.

So I answered them: our fathers, God have mercy on them, did not have God's blessing upon them as His blessing upon us. Therefore: can any of you live today upon what his grandfather lived upon a hundred years ago or fifty years ago? They said: no. I said: can he wear what he used to wear and live by what he used to live by and ride what he used to ride? They said: no. I said: then you are not content with what they were in of worldly things, and you are content with it in religion. Is this not manifest short-measuring? Malik said in the Muwaṭṭaʾ: it is said that everything has its full measure and its short measure. They said: yes. I said: your case and the case of your fathers is like one who took a small child's clothes and wanted to wear them while he is a big man of huge build, and said: this person wears these, and he is a person like me; I have no limb extra to his limbs — but your sizes are different.

And the second answer is that you have met and seen of the kinds of novelties and innovations and problems what your fathers did not see, for they were at a remove and in safety from that. And I asked them: did your fathers expect that the whole community would live by usurious gain? They said: no. Have you yourselves seen that? They said: yes. Did your fathers expect that a son of Muslims would live between his two Muslim parents and reach twenty years of age and behold, he is an atheist who believes neither in God nor in the Last Day and holds what Marx and the other atheists hold? They said: no. I said: has this happened in your own lifetime? They said: yes, we bear witness by God that it has happened. And I kept on with them by degrees until they acknowledged the reality they are in and its difference from what their fathers were upon.

So I said: then do you not recall the saying of Malik, may God have mercy on him: there arise for people judgements according to the dissoluteness they bring about? They said: yes, he said it. I said: dissoluteness has arisen, so bring about judgements for it; and nothing can stop it but what we are engaged in. So they agreed with us on it and said: yes, we agree with you now.

I said: this that you are in has another parallel as well. Your case and your fathers' case in this question is like the case of a people on top of a mountain and a people in the course of a flood. The flood came on with its roaring, and those in its course were addressed by people saying: build a dam, lest the flood tear away your buildings. And they say: no; those on top of the mountain, we see that they do not do this work and do not build a dam, and we do only what they do. And it is said to them: those are at a remove from the flood and it will not reach them, and you are in its direct course. So likewise you and your fathers: they were at a remove from these novelties and you are in their course, so you cannot draw an analogy with them. And they were satisfied with this and content with it. And so it is said to these people in all the fields of the sciences.

As for the bringing of information to mind at the appropriate moment, it is only by two things. The first: that a person should grasp it completely and take it in. For the one who hears the information and supposes that it has stuck to the innermost of his heart is deluded; information is not fixed except by much reviewing and mutual rehearsal and by deliberately recalling it at other than the time of need, so that he may recall it at the time of need. You are most in need of recalling the word of testimony, "there is no god but God, Muhammad is the Messenger of God"; and when a person is in the death throes, this information often fails him and he does not recall it — except those whom God has had mercy upon and granted success and made firm: {God makes firm those who believe with the firm word in the life of this world and in the hereafter} (Sūrat Ibrāhīm 14:27). But whoever remembers God much, and does much of that in the times of health and leisure, will remember Him at the time of hardship. So there must be much recalling of information.

Second, there must be training in bringing information to mind, and that is by the mutual rehearsal of students of knowledge, and by a person's reviewing of his information and the attaining of the links between its parts, so as to activate the mind so that it brings to mind anything deposited in it and knows its place. Like one who puts many items in his house: if his affairs are ordered, then when he comes wanting one of these items he will not go to a room it is not in, but will go to the room he put it in and know its place in it. And likewise if you go and buy books and put them on the shelves and do not read them privately and do not study in them, you will not find your way to the book at the appropriate moment; but if this book is always in your hands and you read it, you know its place, so that even if you do not see it, it is present in your mind and pictured in it in its place. And likewise information: if it is fixed and a person is able to know the way of bringing it to mind, he recalls it as though he saw it written before him — so that if you want to present any piece of information, it is as though you saw it and were reading it, with the page and the volume in the book; you bring it to mind with complete presence.

That is why al-Badawi, may God have mercy on him, said in the versification of ʿAmūd al-Nasab:

*And if you know the momentous lineage, and a biography, you will be well acquainted with them,*

*until it is as though, by the eye of the ink upon the parchment, they had appeared to the eye of the senses.*

He says: if you know the momentous lineage of great import — the lineage of the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, and of his Companions — and a biography, that is, their biographies, you will be well acquainted with them, until it is as though by the eye of the ink (and that is the writing fluid) upon the parchment (and that is the sheet) they had appeared to the eye of the senses — as if you knew them by their colours and their persons.

flags.note: TRANSLATION NOTE. The whole force of this line is that it packs the seven conditions the Sheikh has just expounded into seven imperative verbs. The English renders the seven verbs in order — go abroad, be humble, be scrupulous, be hungry, be weak, disobey your desire, follow — so that a reader can match them one by one to the seven numbered conditions above. 'وهن' (be weak) corresponds to the fifth condition, holding oneself cheap for the sake of knowledge, and 'واتبع' (follow) to the seventh, acting upon it; neither correspondence is obvious from the verb alone, and a reviewer may wish to consider a gloss in the display.

flags.note: TRANSLATION NOTE. The lecture uses several classical Arabic proverbs whose force is lost in a literal English rendering and which the Sheikh does not gloss. 'أطرق كرى إن النعام في القرى' is a rebuke to one who presumes above his station; 'تكاثرت الظباء على خراش' is said when so much comes at once that nothing can be dealt with; 'لا يتزبب قبل أن يتحصرم' is to become a raisin before being a sour grape, that is, to claim maturity prematurely. All are rendered literally, with no English proverb substituted, since substitution would replace the Sheikh's own idiom. 'توما الحكيم' is left as Thomas the sage; the reference is not certain and no identification has been supplied.

translator_notes: Qur'anic renderings in this file are interpretive translations of meaning, offered to carry the Sheikh's argument in English. They are not a substitute for the Arabic text of the Qur'an.

This is tape ONE of the Sheikh's course on the Islamic religious sciences (see IDs 449, 450, 451, 452, 453, 454 for other tapes). It is the introductory lecture: the standing of knowledge, the seven conditions for attaining it, the difference between received knowledge and practised skill, how to prepare oneself to teach, and how to order the sciences — followed by one question and a long answer on why the ancillary sciences exist at all.

The Sheikh's own framing is preserved throughout: he numbers the seven conditions explicitly, and the English carries those numbers in small capitals so that the structure of the lecture is visible, which the running Arabic paragraphing obscures. No headings have been added that he does not speak.

Hadith attributions are kept exactly as given — 'established in the two Ṣaḥīḥs', 'al-Bukhari brought out in suspended form and Ibn Abi ʿAsim connected it', 'al-Bayhaqi in the Sunan and Abu ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-Barr in the introduction to al-Tamhīd and al-Hafiz al-Baghdadi in Sharaf Aṣḥāb al-Ḥadīth by eleven routes, and the Imam Ahmad declared it sound'. Where he gives no attribution, as with the report on God guaranteeing the seeker's provision and the reports about archery, none has been added, and no grading has been supplied anywhere.

'الورع' is rendered 'scrupulousness' throughout, not 'piety' or 'abstinence'; it is the technical term for guarding against the doubtful, which is exactly what the hadith of al-Nuʿman ibn Bashir, quoted at length here, establishes. 'علم لدني' is 'knowledge bestowed directly', keeping the Qur'anic resonance of ʿilm min ladunnā without importing 'mystical'.

The wordplay on 'علم بالجِد وعلم بالجَد' — knowledge by earnest effort and knowledge by good fortune, two words differing only in a vowel — cannot be reproduced in English. The two senses are given with the transliteration in brackets so that the pun is visible rather than lost.

The record is a single continuous session with no second opening formula, unlike tapes twelve and fourteen; and the page carries no download link, so it is not an excerpt-only record under house rule 9. Its one structural defect is the announced final section that never arrives.
